Effective Context in Transformers: An Analysis of Fragmentation and Tokenization

Amirmehdi J. Fesharaki Affiliation: Department of Communications and Electronics Affiliation: Institut Polytechnique de Paris Email: amirmehdi.jafari@ip-paris.fr    Mohammadamin Rami Affiliation: Department of Communications and Electronics Affiliation: Institut Polytechnique de Paris Email: mohammadamin.rami@ip-paris.fr    Aslan Tchamkerten Affiliation: Department of Communications and Electronics Affiliation: Institut Polytechnique de Paris Email: aslan.tchamkerten@telecom-paris.fr
Abstract

Transformers predict over a representation of a sequence. The same data can be written as bytes, characters, or subword tokens, and these representations may be lossless. Yet, under a fixed context window, they need not expose the same information to the model. This raises a basic question: how does the choice of representation change what a finite-context predictor can achieve?

We study this question on Markov sources and uncover two complementary phenomena. First, we observe that moving to smaller representation units can hurt prediction even when the context window is enlarged to cover the relevant source history. To explain this, we introduce fragmentation: a lossless recoding that replaces each source symbol by several smaller units. We prove that fragmentation can strictly increase the optimal finite-context log-loss, showing that the gap is not merely an optimization or capacity issue, but can be intrinsic to the representation. This gives a theoretical account of the finite-context gap observed in byte- and character-level models such as ByT5 and CANINE relative to subword-tokenized models. Second, we study the opposite direction: greedy tokenization—BPE, WordPiece, and related methods—which groups source symbols into larger units. We show that tokenization can make a short token window behave like a longer source-context window, and we give a loss guarantee describing when this is achievable. The guarantee depends on how reliably token windows span the needed source history, together with the compression rate of the tokenizer. This also yields a simple diagnostic for real tokenizers: measuring how much source context a fixed token window reliably contains. Together, the two directions establish a finite-context information-theoretic framework for reasoning about representation choices in Transformers.

1 Introduction

Sequence prediction is at the core of modern language modeling, and the Transformer architecture has proven remarkably effective for this task (Vaswani et al., 2017, Devlin et al., 2019, Brown et al., 2020, Touvron et al., 2023). Most analyses of these models focus on architecture, optimization, scaling, or data. Yet there is a more basic choice made before training begins: how the sequence is represented. The same text can be represented as bytes, characters, words, or subword tokens. These encodings may be lossless, but a fixed model window over them can cover very different amounts of the original sequence. Thus, even lossless representations can lead to different finite-context prediction problems.

This tension appears directly in modern language modeling. Token-free models such as ByT5 and CANINE avoid a fixed subword tokenizer by operating on bytes or characters, but they must process longer sequences and face a more expensive context problem (Xue et al., 2022, Clark et al., 2022). Other approaches reduce this cost using latent subword blocks or multiscale byte-level modeling (Tay et al., 2021, Yu et al., 2023). At the same time, most mainstream language models still use a fixed discrete tokenizer learned before model training, often based on subword or byte-level variants of BPE, WordPiece, or unigram language-model tokenization (Sennrich et al., 2016, Schuster and Nakajima, 2012, Devlin et al., 2019, Kudo and Richardson, 2018). This creates a basic representation tradeoff: token-free models avoid committing to a fixed tokenizer, but they operate on longer sequences; tokenized models shorten the sequence, but they introduce a preprocessing choice which changes the prediction problem.

To study this tradeoff cleanly, we focus on finite-context prediction on stationary finite-order Markov sources. In this setting, the relevant history is explicit: once the context reaches the Markov order, the optimal finite-context loss reaches the entropy rate. This lets us isolate how the representation changes what is available inside a fixed window. We ask:

How does representation shape what a finite-context predictor can achieve?

We show that this question has two sides. Moving to smaller representation units can make prediction harder, even when the recoding is lossless. Moving to larger token units can make the same finite window carry more information about the original source. The paper formalizes both effects and identifies the quantities that determine when they arise. In short, our contributions are:

  • •

    We uncover a fragmentation effect motivated by Figure 1: when a source is recoded into sub-symbol units, a transformer can converge to a strictly worse loss even after its window is enlarged to cover the relevant source history. This mirrors the prediction problem faced by byte- or character-level models. We formalize the effect as a lossless recoding into smaller units and prove that the resulting excess loss can be intrinsic to the representation.

  • •

    We develop a finite-context analysis of greedy tokenization. We show that if a token window spans enough source symbols, then a token-level predictor can match the performance of a longer source-context predictor with no asymptotic loss. We then extend this to typical token windows, giving an achievability bound controlled by the lower tail of the source-span distribution and the tokenizer compression rate.

  • •

    We identify the effective source context of a tokenizer as a measurable quantity for finite-context prediction. The theory lets us compare tokenizers by the guarantees they provide: for a fixed token window, which tokenizer can reliably match a source-level predictor with the largest possible context, up to small excess loss? This criterion depends on the lower tail of the token-window source-span distribution, not on average token length alone.

1.1 Related Work

Beyond the standard tokenizer algorithms cited above, recent work studies tokenization as a modeling and efficiency choice. Goldman et al. (2024) connect tokenizer compression to downstream model performance, while Tao et al. (Tao et al., 2024) study how vocabulary size should scale with model size and compute. Other work highlights limitations of fixed subword tokenization, including robustness failures and sensitivity to token structure (Chai et al., 2024), as well as broader effects on meaning, reasoning, and multilingual efficiency  (Haslett, 2025, Zhang et al., 2025). Our results are complementary: rather than evaluating tokenizer choices empirically, we characterize how a lossless representation changes the best achievable finite-context loss.

The closest theoretical line studies Transformers and related sequence models on Markov sources (Makkuva et al., 2024, Rajaraman et al., 2024b, Rajaraman et al., 2024a, Edelman et al., 2024, Bondaschi et al., 2025). These works use Markov data as a controlled setting to reveal what sequence models learn in context. In particular,  (Makkuva et al., 2024) show that single-layer Transformers can behave like unigram predictors on higher-order Markov chains, while  (Rajaraman et al., 2024b) show that tokenization can make a unigram-style predictor near-optimal under suitable learned dictionaries. Our work stays in the Transformer finite-context view, but shifts the question from model behavior to representation: how does a lossless recoding change the best loss achievable by any fixed-window predictor?

Finally, our greedy tokenizer model is related to dictionary parsing and compression, including Lempel–Ziv and LZW methods  (Ziv and Lempel, 1977, Ziv and Lempel, 1978, Welch, 1984), and recent compression/coding views of tokenization  (Zouhar et al., 2023, Schmidt et al., 2024). Both settings trade vocabulary size for longer emitted units; we translate this tradeoff into an achievability guarantee based on the source-span distribution of token windows.

2 Background

Throughout the paper, {Yi}i∈ℤ\{Y_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{Z}} is an ergodic stationary finite order-kk Markov process defined over a finite alphabet 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. Recall that a process {Yi}i∈ℤ\{Y_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{Z}} is kkth-order Markov if, for every ii, Pr⁡(Yi∣Y−∞i−1)=Pr⁡(Yi∣Yi−ki−1)almost surely\Pr(Y_{i}\mid Y_{-\infty}^{i-1})=\Pr(Y_{i}\mid Y_{i-k}^{i-1})\quad\text{almost surely}. We shall also encounter processes that are not stationary but retain a periodic form of stationarity. A process {Xi}i∈ℤ\{X_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{Z}} is cyclostationary with period MM if its finite-dimensional distributions are invariant under shifts by multiples of MM: (Xi1,…,Xim)​=𝑑​(Xi1+M,…,Xim+M)(X_{i_{1}},\ldots,X_{i_{m}})\overset{d}{=}(X_{i_{1}+M},\ldots,X_{i_{m}+M}) for all mm and all indices i1,…,imi_{1},\ldots,i_{m}. Such processes arise when each symbol of a stationary source is represented by a block of MM subsymbols.

2.1 Finite-Context Predictors

We study predictors that, at time ii, observe only a finite suffix of the past and assign a probability to the next symbol. For an integer w≥0w\geq 0, a ww-context predictor is a collection of probability distributions on 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, one for each context c∈𝒴wc\in\mathcal{Y}^{w}. Equivalently, it is a map q:𝒴×𝒴w→[0,1],satisfying​∑y∈𝒴q⁡(y∣c)=1,c∈𝒴w.q:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}^{w}\to[0,1],\;\text{satisfying}\;\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}q(y\mid c)=1,\;c\in\mathcal{Y}^{w}. We denote the class of all such predictors by 𝒬w𝒴\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{Y}}. Given q∈𝒬w𝒴q\in\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{Y}}, its population log-loss on the source {Yi}\{Y_{i}\} is LY​(q):=𝔼⁡[−log2⁡q⁡(Y0∣Y−w−1)].L_{Y}(q):=\mathbb{E}\left[-\log_{2}q\!\left(Y_{0}\mid Y_{-w}^{-1}\right)\right]. The minimum loss with context length ww is then

ℒY​(w):=minq∈𝒬w𝒴⁡LY​(q).\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w):=\min_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{Y}}}L_{Y}(q). (1)

For completeness, recall that if qq has finite expected log-loss, then Birkhoff’s ergodic theorem (see, e.g., Cover and Thomas (2005)) yields 1nℓ(q;Yn)⟶n→∞LY(q)a.s.,whereℓ(q;Yn):=∑i=w+1n−log2q(Yi∣Yi−wi−1),\frac{1}{n}\ell(q;Y^{n})\overset{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}L_{Y}(q)\;\text{a.s.,}\;\text{where}\;\ell(q;Y^{n}):=\sum_{i=w+1}^{n}-\log_{2}q\!\left(Y_{i}\mid Y_{i-w}^{i-1}\right), i.e., the population loss is the almost-sure asymptotic normalized log-loss along “typical” realizations.

Specializing to our Markovian source, the optimal ww-context loss is ℒY​(w)=H⁡(Y0∣Y−w−1),\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w)=H(Y_{0}\mid Y_{-w}^{-1}), which is a non-increasing function of ww—since conditioning reduces entropy. In particular, once the context length reaches the Markov order, i.e., w≥kw\geq k, the minimum loss becomes ℒY​(w)=H⁡(Y0∣Y−k−1).\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w)=H(Y_{0}\mid Y_{-k}^{-1}).

All logarithms are base 22, unless specified otherwise. For any alphabet 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, the set 𝒴∗\mathcal{Y}^{*} is defined as 𝒴∗=⋃n≥0𝒴n\mathcal{Y}^{*}=\bigcup_{n\geq 0}\mathcal{Y}^{n}.

3 Can Lossless Recoding Hurt Finite-Context Prediction?

We first examine the effect of refining the representation. We call this operation fragmentation: each source symbol is replaced, losslessly, by a short string over a smaller alphabet. This idealizes the passage from words or characters to bytes or bits.

Fragmentation preserves the source sequence, but not necessarily the information available at finite context. A finite-context predictor sees only a fixed window in the chosen representation. After fragmentation, this window may cut through source-symbol boundaries, obscure the phase of the next fragment within its source symbol, and fail to contain the source history available before fragmentation. Thus a globally lossless refinement can nevertheless increase finite-context prediction loss.

Fragmentation can hurt even with sufficient context.

Figure 1 gives a first indication of the effect. We generate a stationary Markov source of order kk and compare two predictors with the same architecture. One predicts the source symbols directly from a context of length ww. The other predicts a fragmented representation: each source symbol is replaced by a block of MM smaller symbols, and the context length is enlarged to M​wMw.

Note that we choose w>kw>k. Hence the source-level predictor sees the entire Markov state. The fragmented predictor, in turn, sees M​wMw fragments, the nominal span of ww source symbols. On this accounting, the two predictors should have access to the same amount of relevant history, and one might expect the same limiting loss, measured in bits per source symbol.

They do not. The fragmented predictor converges to a strictly larger loss. The gap persists after training has stabilized, and therefore is not merely an optimization transient or an artifact of insufficient capacity. It is a property of the representation. Fragmentation changes the finite-context prediction problem: even when the window is long enough in source-symbol units, it may not reveal the phase of the next fragment nor align with the source history used by the unfragmented predictor. The remainder of this section explains this gap.

We first formalize fragmentation:

In what follows, context lengths for the fragmented process are measured in 𝒳\mathcal{X}-symbols, i.e., in fragments. Thus a window of length M​wMw in the fragmented process has the same nominal span as ww source symbols.

Example.

Let 𝒴={a,b,c,d}\mathcal{Y}=\{a,b,c,d\}, and fragment each source symbol into two bits by φ⁡(a)=00,φ⁡(b)=01,φ⁡(c)=10,φ⁡(d)=11.\varphi(a)=00,\qquad\varphi(b)=01,\qquad\varphi(c)=10,\qquad\varphi(d)=11. Each bit of the fragmented process has one of two phases: it is either the first or the second bit of the encoded source symbol; see Figure 2. Suppose that {Yi}\{Y_{i}\} is first-order Markov, and consider a bit predictor with context length 33. This context always contains a complete preceding two-bit block. Yet it need not determine the phase of the bit to be predicted. Figure 2 shows two occurrences of the same bit context, 101101.

In Case 11, the context ends at a block boundary, so the next bit is the first bit of a new source symbol, distributed according to the Markov transition from the previous symbol. In Case 22, the context ends inside a block, so the next bit completes the current source symbol; after observing first bit 11, the symbol is restricted to cc or dd. The predictor, however, only observes the context string 101101 and not the phase at which it occurs. It must therefore assign the same next-bit distribution in both cases, even though the correct conditional distributions may differ. This phase mismatch creates the excess loss quantified below.

To state the gap, we put both losses on the same scale: bits per original source symbol. Let 𝒬w𝒳\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{X}} be the class of ww-context predictors on the fragmented alphabet 𝒳\mathcal{X}, where ww is measured in fragments. For a source block Y1nY_{1}^{n}, write

φ(Y1n):=φ(Y1)φ(Y2)⋯φ(Yn)∈𝒳M​n\varphi(Y_{1}^{n}):=\varphi(Y_{1})\varphi(Y_{2})\cdots\varphi(Y_{n})\in\mathcal{X}^{Mn}

for the corresponding fragmented string. For q∈𝒬w𝒳q\in\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{X}}, define its fragmented population loss by LXfrag​(q):=∑θ=1M𝔼⁡[−log2⁡q⁡(Xθ∣Xθ−wθ−1)].L_{X}^{\mathrm{frag}}(q):=\sum_{\theta=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\log_{2}q\!\left(X_{\theta}\mid X_{\theta-w}^{\theta-1}\right)\right]. The expectation in the θ\thetath term is taken at phase θ\theta. By stationarity of {Yi}\{Y_{i}\}, the fragmented process is cyclostationary with period MM, so the distribution of each phase-θ\theta term is independent of the source-symbol index. Thus LXfrag​(q)L_{X}^{\mathrm{frag}}(q) is the expected cumulative log-loss incurred in predicting the MM fragments of one source symbol.11 1 If LXfrag​(q)<∞L_{X}^{\mathrm{frag}}(q)<\infty, then Birkhoff’s theorem applied to the stationary block process yields n−1​ℓ​(q,φ⁡(Y1n))→LXfrag​(q)n^{-1}\ell(q;\varphi(Y_{1}^{n}))\to L_{X}^{\mathrm{frag}}(q) almost surely. The optimal fragmented loss with context length ww is

ℒXfrag​(w):=minq∈𝒬w𝒳⁡LXfrag​(q).\mathcal{L}_{X}^{\mathrm{frag}}(w):=\min_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{X}}}L_{X}^{\mathrm{frag}}(q). (2)

We compare ℒXfrag​(M​w)\mathcal{L}_{X}^{\mathrm{frag}}(Mw) with ℒY​(w)\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w) because M​wMw fragments have the same nominal span as ww source symbols, and both losses are measured in bits per source symbol. A source predictor assigns probability directly to YiY_{i}, while a fragmented predictor assigns probability to the same symbol through its MM fragments. The comparison is nontrivial because the fragmented window need not align with source-symbol boundaries. The next result quantifies the resulting excess loss; the proof is given in Appendix A.1.

Since both terms are nonnegative, ℒXfrag​(M​w)≥ℒY​(w).\mathcal{L}_{X}^{\mathrm{frag}}(Mw)\geq\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w). Thus, a lossless finer representation can strictly increase the optimal finite-context prediction loss.

Proof idea.

A fragmented predictor conditions only on the last M​wMw fragments. Hence two occurrences with the same fragment context are treated identically, even if they occur at different phases. Equivalently, its optimal loss is the loss of a prediction problem in which the phase of the prediction time is first randomized and then hidden from the predictor. Comparing this phase-hidden loss with the chain-rule expansion of the source-level loss separates the gap into two terms: the information needed to identify the phase, and the source history lost because the fragmented window is not aligned with source-symbol boundaries.

Implication for byte- and character-level models.

Theorem 3.1 gives a possible explanation for the finite-context gap between byte- or character-level models, such as ByT5 (Xue et al., 2022) and CANINE (Clark et al., 2022), and tokenized models. Such models represent a source unit as a sequence of symbols in a finer alphabet. Even when the model is well trained, and even when its window has the nominal span needed to cover the relevant source history, the local prediction problem may remain harder. The same fragment context can arise at different positions inside the original source unit, and these positions can induce different conditional distributions for the next fragment. The resulting loss is therefore not merely an optimization or capacity effect; it can be intrinsic to the representation.

There is a second cost. Finer representations lengthen the sequence. To cover the same amount of source history, a byte- or character-level model needs a longer context window than a token-level model. For Transformers, this increase is expensive. Token-free models must therefore either pay the longer-sequence cost directly (Xue et al., 2022), or reduce it through architectural mechanisms such as downsampling (Clark et al., 2022). This points to the complementary question studied next: when source symbols are grouped into tokens, what property of the tokenizer determines how much source history a fixed token window contains?

4 When Does Tokenization Extend Effective Context?

We now consider the reverse transformation. Tokenization groups consecutive source symbols into units from a larger alphabet. Its advantage is that a fixed number of tokens may cover more source history than the same number of source symbols, thereby reducing finite-context loss.

However, this gain is not automatic. A token predictor conditions on the output of an encoder, and under greedy tokenization the relevant token boundaries may depend on symbols not yet predicted. Thus, token history is not merely a reblocking of source history. We need conditions under which a short token context contains enough determined history to emulate a longer source-context predictor.

Empirical observation.

Figure 3 shows the phenomenon studied in this section. We use a binary stationary Markov source of order k=12k=12. On the original sequence, a Transformer needs a window of length 1212 to reach the entropy rate. After tokenization, the same architecture can reach the entropy rate with a shorter token window, despite predicting over a larger alphabet. As the token vocabulary grows, the limiting loss decreases and approaches the entropy rate.

This section explains when such a gain is possible. The question is when a short token context carries enough determined source history to match a longer source-context predictor, and how much loss is incurred when it does not.

Greedy tokenization.

We model a tokenizer as a prefix-closed finite vocabulary of source strings, organized as a prefix tree, together with a greedy parser. The vocabulary 𝒵⊂𝒴∗\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathcal{Y}^{*} contains all single-symbol strings in 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, namely 𝒴⊂𝒵\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathcal{Z}. Given a source sequence y1ny_{1}^{n}, greedy tokenization scans from left to right and emits the longest vocabulary string matching the remaining source sequence. We write

z1m=Π𝒵​(y1n)z_{1}^{m}=\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}}(y_{1}^{n})

for the resulting token sequence. We also define the expansion (decoding) map Γ𝒵:𝒵∗→𝒴∗\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}:\mathcal{Z}^{*}\to\mathcal{Y}^{*}, which maps a token sequence back to the underlying source sequence by concatenating the source strings represented by its tokens. Thus,

Γ𝒵(z1m)=Γ𝒵(z1)Γ𝒵(z2)⋯Γ𝒵(zm),\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{1}^{m})=\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{1})\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{2})\cdots\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{m}),

and, for every source sequence, Γ𝒵​(Π𝒵​(y1n))=y1n.\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}\!\left(\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}}(y_{1}^{n})\right)=y_{1}^{n}.

This abstraction captures the core parsing mechanism behind many practical dictionary and subword tokenizers: a learned vocabulary constrains which strings can be emitted, and the parser segments the input into vocabulary elements. It covers classical dictionary methods such as LZW (Zouhar et al., 2023), and is a useful model for greedy subword tokenizers such as WordPiece (Devlin et al., 2019) and variants of Byte Pair Encoding (Sennrich et al., 2016).

Source span of a token window.

We can now make the context-extension intuition precise. A token predictor does not directly condition on source symbols; it conditions on the last ww tokens. The relevant question is how much source history those tokens actually contain. For a token string zi−wi−1z_{i-w}^{i-1}, define its source span S:𝒵∗→ℕS:\mathcal{Z}^{*}\to\mathbb{N} by

S⁡(zi−wi−1):=|Γ𝒵​(zi−wi−1)|.S(z_{i-w}^{i-1}):=\left|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-w}^{i-1})\right|.

In particular, S⁡(zi−wi−1)S(z_{i-w}^{i-1}) is the number of original source symbols contained in the token context seen by the predictor.

To compare token-level and source-level prediction, we again measure loss in bits per original source symbol. Let 𝒬w𝒵\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{Z}} denote the class of ww-context predictors over the token alphabet 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Note that stationarity and ergodicity of {Yi}\{Y_{i}\} implies that {Zj}\{Z_{j}\} is also stationary and ergodic.22 2 A one-sided greedy parse has an initial-boundary artifact, since the first token is forced to start at the origin. Throughout, {Zj}\{Z_{j}\} denotes the stationary version obtained by looking at the parse from a typical emitted-token boundary. Equivalently, the expectations below can be read as long-run empirical averages along a long greedy parse, with boundary effects ignored. For q~∈𝒬w𝒵\tilde{q}\in\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{Z}}, define

LZtok​(q~):=𝔼⁡[−log2⁡q~​(Z0∣Z−w−1)]𝔼⁡[|Γ𝒵​(Z0)|].L_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(\tilde{q}):=\frac{\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\log_{2}\tilde{q}\!\left(Z_{0}\mid Z_{-w}^{-1}\right)\right]}{\mathbb{E}\!\left[|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(Z_{0})|\right]}.

The denominator converts token-level loss into bits per source symbol. The optimal tokenized loss with context length ww is

ℒZtok​(w):=minq~∈𝒬w𝒵⁡LZtok​(q~).\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(w):=\min_{\tilde{q}\in\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{Z}}}L_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(\tilde{q}).

We now ask when the source span of a token window can be turned into an actual prediction guarantee. For a fixed token-window length ww, define the worst-case source span

ws​(w):=min⁡{S⁡(z1w):z1w​ is a valid length-w token window}.w_{s}(w):=\min\left\{S(z_{1}^{w}):z_{1}^{w}\text{ is a valid length-$w$ token window}\right\}.

Thus every valid ww-token context contains at least ws​(w)w_{s}(w) source symbols. This means that the token history contains the source history used by a ws​(w)w_{s}(w)-context source predictor.

However, this containment alone does not give a token-level predictor. A source predictor assigns probabilities one source symbol at a time, while a token predictor must assign probabilities to entire tokens. Moreover, under greedy parsing, not every source string that has positive probability can be emitted as the next token: shorter strings may be suppressed when they are prefixes of longer matching vocabulary elements. Thus, one must construct a valid distribution over next tokens whose cumulative probability along the greedy parse matches the source-level predictor.

The next theorem shows that this can be done exactly. Any source predictor with context length ws​(w)w_{s}(w), with some mild assumptions, can be converted into a ww-token predictor whose cumulative log-loss matches the source-level cumulative log-loss up to an additive O⁡(1)O(1) term independent of the sequence length.

The proof is constructive, deferred to Appendix A.2.

The theorem shows that source span is not only an intuitive measure of context length; it is enough to transfer prediction rules. Whenever every ww-token window spans at least wsw_{s} source symbols, a ww-token predictor can reproduce the behavior of any wsw_{s}-context source predictor, with no asymptotic loss.

This immediately gives a guarantee on the optimal token-level loss.

— the proof is given in Appendix A.3

For a kkth-order Markov source, ℒY​(ws)\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w_{s}) reaches the entropy rate once ws≥kw_{s}\geq k. Thus a token predictor with window w<kw<k can still achieve the Markov optimum, provided that its ww tokens always span at least kk source symbols. This explains the empirical observation: Even though greedy parsing introduces boundary-dependent constraints on which tokens can appear next, these constraints do not prevent transfer — a token-level predictor can still match the loss of a source-level predictor with the corresponding extended source context.

From worst-case to typical span.

The deterministic condition above captures the mechanism, but it is too stringent for practical tokenizers. Real vocabularies contain short tokens, often including single-symbol tokens. Hence the worst-case span of a ww-token window may be small even when most windows cover much more source history. To capture this behavior, we relax the span requirement: instead of requiring every ww-token window to cover wsw_{s} source symbols, we require this with high probability.

Here ϵ\epsilon is the probability that a ww-token context fails to contain wsw_{s} source symbols. When ϵ=0\epsilon=0, The deterministic setting of Corollary 4.2 is recovered. When ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the transfer may fail on a small fraction of windows, and the loss guarantee must pay for those failures. To express this penalty per source symbol, we define the expected token length α𝒵:=𝔼⁡[|Γ𝒵​(Z0)|]\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}:=\mathbb{E}\!\left[|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(Z_{0})|\right] and the tokenizer compression rate

R𝒵:=log2⁡|𝒵|α𝒵​log2​|𝒴|.R_{\mathcal{Z}}:=\frac{\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}\log_{2}|\mathcal{Y}|}.

Thus R𝒵R_{\mathcal{Z}} is the uniform-code rate of the tokenizer, measured in units of source-symbol bits.

Interpretation.

Theorem 4.3 converts a typical-span statement into a prediction guarantee. For a fixed token window ww, one may choose the largest source span wsw_{s} for which the slack ϵ⁡(w,ws)​R𝒵​log2​|𝒴|\epsilon(w,w_{s})R_{\mathcal{Z}}\log_{2}|\mathcal{Y}| remains small. The theorem then shows that the best ww-context token predictor matches a wsw_{s}-context source predictor up to this slack. In this sense, wsw_{s} is an effective source context supplied by the tokenizer at window length ww. The proof is deferred to Appendix A.4.

Existence under a vocabulary budget.

The typical-span condition is not only a diagnostic. In Appendix B, we show under heavy-hitting assumptions for learned greedy tokenizers as in (Rajaraman et al., 2024b), a budget-dd greedy tokenizer can satisfy the typical-span condition with a target source span that grows like w​log⁡dw\log d. Thus, increasing the vocabulary budget can provably make a fixed ww-token window simulate a much longer source-context window, up to the slack term in Thm 4.3.

5 Open Questions and Limitations

Our results isolate an achievable-loss effect, but not the full optimization or expressivity picture for trained Transformers. The predictor-transfer arguments construct finite-context predictors, but they do not show that a Transformer architecture can realize them, or that training will find them. In Appendix D.2, tokenization appears to improve convergence speed; explaining this remains open.

Our theory also gives a criterion for tokenizer quality, not a complete tokenizer-design method. It suggests that average token length is insufficient: the lower tail of the source-span distribution matters. This motivates training tokenizers to optimize effective context while balancing vocabulary size, output-layer cost, and rare-token effects.

6 Conclusion

We studied how lossless representations affect finite-context prediction. Fragmentation can hurt by introducing phase ambiguity and missing source history, even though the original sequence is recoverable. This gives a theoretical account of the finite-context gap observed in byte- and character-level models such as ByT5 and CANINE relative to subword-tokenized models. Tokenization—BPE, WordPiece, and related methods—can have the opposite effect: a short token window can behave like a longer source window when it reliably spans enough source symbols. Together, the results show that the relevant quantity for Transformers is not only raw context length, but the effective source context exposed by the representation.

Appendix A Proof of Theorems

A.1 Proof of Theorem 3.1

Proof.

Recall that the process {Xj}j∈ℤ\{X_{j}\}_{j\in\mathbb{Z}} is cyclostationary with period MM. Indeed, shifting the fragmented process by MM positions corresponds exactly to shifting the original source process by one symbol while preserving the phase within each fragmented block. Since {Yi}\{Y_{i}\} is stationary, for any indices j1,…,jrj_{1},\ldots,j_{r},

(Xj1,…,Xjr)​=𝑑​(Xj1+M,…,Xjr+M).(X_{j_{1}},\ldots,X_{j_{r}})\overset{d}{=}(X_{j_{1}+M},\ldots,X_{j_{r}+M}).

We now randomize the phase. Let Θ\Theta be uniform on {1,…,M}\{1,\ldots,M\}, independent of {Xj}\{X_{j}\}, and define

Xj′:=Xj+Θ,j∈ℤ.X^{\prime}_{j}:=X_{j+\Theta},\qquad j\in\mathbb{Z}.

By the law of total probability over Θ\Theta,

Pr⁡(Xj1′=x1,…,Xjr′=xr)\displaystyle\Pr\!\left(X^{\prime}_{j_{1}}=x_{1},\ldots,X^{\prime}_{j_{r}}=x_{r}\right)
=∑θ=1MPr(Xj1+θ=x1,…,Xjr+θ=xr|Θ=θ)Pr(Θ=θ).\displaystyle\qquad=\sum_{\theta=1}^{M}\Pr\!\left(X_{j_{1}+\theta}=x_{1},\ldots,X_{j_{r}+\theta}=x_{r}\,\middle|\,\Theta=\theta\right)\Pr(\Theta=\theta).

Since Θ\Theta is independent of {Xj}\{X_{j}\} and uniform on {1,…,M}\{1,\ldots,M\}, this gives

Pr⁡(Xj1′=x1,…,Xjr′=xr)\displaystyle\Pr\!\left(X^{\prime}_{j_{1}}=x_{1},\ldots,X^{\prime}_{j_{r}}=x_{r}\right)
=1M​∑θ=1MPr⁡(Xj1+θ=x1,…,Xjr+θ=xr).\displaystyle\qquad=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{\theta=1}^{M}\Pr\!\left(X_{j_{1}+\theta}=x_{1},\ldots,X_{j_{r}+\theta}=x_{r}\right).

Thus the joint distribution of {Xj′}\{X^{\prime}_{j}\} is obtained by averaging over the MM phases of the cyclostationary process {Xj}\{X_{j}\}. Since shifting all indices of X′X^{\prime} only permutes these MM phase classes, {Xj′}\{X^{\prime}_{j}\} is stationary.

For any q∈𝒬M​w𝒳q\in\mathcal{Q}_{Mw}^{\mathcal{X}}, by definition,

LXfrag​(q)=∑θ=1M𝔼⁡[−log2⁡q⁡(Xθ∣Xθ−M​wθ−1)].L_{X}^{\mathrm{frag}}(q)=\sum_{\theta=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\log_{2}q\!\left(X_{\theta}\mid X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right)\right].

Using the phase-randomized process, by the law of total expectation,

𝔼⁡[−log2⁡q⁡(X0′∣(X′)−M​w−1)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\log_{2}q\!\left(X^{\prime}_{0}\mid(X^{\prime})_{-Mw}^{-1}\right)\right]
=𝔼⁡[−log2⁡q⁡(XΘ∣XΘ−M​wΘ−1)]\displaystyle\qquad=\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\log_{2}q\!\left(X_{\Theta}\mid X_{\Theta-Mw}^{\Theta-1}\right)\right]
=1M​∑θ=1M𝔼⁡[−log2⁡q⁡(Xθ∣Xθ−M​wθ−1)].\displaystyle\qquad=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{\theta=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\log_{2}q\!\left(X_{\theta}\mid X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right)\right].

Therefore,

LXfrag​(q)=M⋅𝔼⁡[−log2⁡q⁡(X0′∣(X′)−M​w−1)].L_{X}^{\mathrm{frag}}(q)=M\cdot\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\log_{2}q\!\left(X^{\prime}_{0}\mid(X^{\prime})_{-Mw}^{-1}\right)\right].

Since {Xj′}\{X^{\prime}_{j}\} is stationary, the optimal M​wMw-context predictor for X′X^{\prime} achieves the conditional entropy. Hence

ℒXfrag​(M​w)=M​H​(X0′∣(X′)−M​w−1)=M​H​(XΘ∣XΘ−M​wΘ−1).\mathcal{L}_{X}^{\mathrm{frag}}(Mw)=MH\!\left(X^{\prime}_{0}\mid(X^{\prime})_{-Mw}^{-1}\right)=MH\!\left(X_{\Theta}\mid X_{\Theta-Mw}^{\Theta-1}\right). (3)

We now express the source-level loss in terms of the fragmented variables. Since φ\varphi is injective, the block X1MX_{1}^{M} contains exactly the same information as Y1Y_{1}, and the block X1−M​w0X_{1-Mw}^{0} contains exactly the same information as Y1−w0Y_{1-w}^{0}. Therefore,

ℒY​(w)=H⁡(Y1∣Y1−w0)=H⁡(X1M∣X1−M​w0).\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w)=H(Y_{1}\mid Y_{1-w}^{0})=H(X_{1}^{M}\mid X_{1-Mw}^{0}).

ℒY​(w)=∑θ=1MH⁡(Xθ∣X1−M​wθ−1).\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w)=\sum_{\theta=1}^{M}H\!\left(X_{\theta}\mid X_{1-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right). (4)

H⁡(XΘ∣XΘ−M​wΘ−1,Θ)=1M​∑θ=1MH⁡(Xθ∣Xθ−M​wθ−1).H\!\left(X_{\Theta}\mid X_{\Theta-Mw}^{\Theta-1},\Theta\right)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{\theta=1}^{M}H\!\left(X_{\theta}\mid X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right).

Therefore,

M​H​(XΘ∣XΘ−M​wΘ−1)−∑θ=1MH⁡(Xθ∣Xθ−M​wθ−1)\displaystyle MH\!\left(X_{\Theta}\mid X_{\Theta-Mw}^{\Theta-1}\right)-\sum_{\theta=1}^{M}H\!\left(X_{\theta}\mid X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right)
=M​I​(Θ;XΘ∣XΘ−M​wΘ−1).\displaystyle\qquad=MI\!\left(\Theta;X_{\Theta}\mid X_{\Theta-Mw}^{\Theta-1}\right). (5)

=[M​H​(XΘ∣XΘ−M​wΘ−1)−∑θ=1MH⁡(Xθ∣Xθ−M​wθ−1)]\displaystyle=\Bigg[MH\!\left(X_{\Theta}\mid X_{\Theta-Mw}^{\Theta-1}\right)-\sum_{\theta=1}^{M}H\!\left(X_{\theta}\mid X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right)\Bigg]
+∑θ=1M[H(Xθ∣Xθ−M​wθ−1)−H(Xθ∣X1−M​wθ−1)].\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{\theta=1}^{M}\Bigg[H\!\left(X_{\theta}\mid X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right)-H\!\left(X_{\theta}\mid X_{1-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right)\Bigg].

The first bracket is the phase-ambiguity term by (5). For the second term, observe that when θ=1\theta=1,

Xθ−M​wθ−1=X1−M​w0=X1−M​wθ−1,X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}=X_{1-Mw}^{0}=X_{1-Mw}^{\theta-1},

so the corresponding difference is zero. For θ≥2\theta\geq 2,

X1−M​wθ−1=(X1−M​wθ−M​w−1,Xθ−M​wθ−1).X_{1-Mw}^{\theta-1}=\left(X_{1-Mw}^{\theta-Mw-1},X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right).

Hence

H⁡(Xθ∣Xθ−M​wθ−1)−H⁡(Xθ∣X1−M​wθ−1)\displaystyle H\!\left(X_{\theta}\mid X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right)-H\!\left(X_{\theta}\mid X_{1-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right)
=I(Xθ;X1−M​wθ−M​w−1|Xθ−M​wθ−1).\displaystyle\qquad=I\!\left(X_{\theta};X_{1-Mw}^{\theta-Mw-1}\,\middle|\,X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right).

Combining the two parts gives

ℒXfrag(Mw)−ℒY(w)=∑θ=2MI(Xθ;X1−M​wθ−M​w−1|Xθ−M​wθ−1)+MI(Θ;XΘ|XΘ−M​wΘ−1),\mathcal{L}_{X}^{\mathrm{frag}}(Mw)-\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w)=\sum_{\theta=2}^{M}I\!\left(X_{\theta};X_{1-Mw}^{\theta-Mw-1}\,\middle|\,X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right)+MI\!\left(\Theta;X_{\Theta}\,\middle|\,X_{\Theta-Mw}^{\Theta-1}\right),

which is the desired decomposition.

It remains to justify the final claim. The context-deficit term measures the information about XθX_{\theta} contained in the missing prefix X1−M​wθ−M​w−1X_{1-Mw}^{\theta-Mw-1} beyond the fragmented context Xθ−M​wθ−1X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}. When w>kw>k, the fragmented context Xθ−M​wθ−1X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1} already contains the last kk complete source symbols before Y1Y_{1}, namely Y1−k0Y_{1-k}^{0}, as well as the previous fragments X1θ−1X_{1}^{\theta-1} of the current symbol. The missing prefix belongs only to source symbols older than this Markov context. Since {Yi}\{Y_{i}\} is kk-th order Markov and XθX_{\theta} is a deterministic function of Y1Y_{1}, the missing prefix carries no additional information about XθX_{\theta} once Xθ−M​wθ−1X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1} is given. Therefore,

I(Xθ;X1−M​wθ−M​w−1|Xθ−M​wθ−1)=0,θ=2,…,M,I\!\left(X_{\theta};X_{1-Mw}^{\theta-Mw-1}\,\middle|\,X_{\theta-Mw}^{\theta-1}\right)=0,\qquad\theta=2,\ldots,M,

whenever w>kw>k. Thus the context-deficit term vanishes for w>kw>k. ∎

A.2 Proof of Theorem 4.1

Proof.

Throughout this proof, we use the prefix-closedness of the vocabulary: whenever z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, every nonempty prefix of zz also belongs to 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Therefore, if a token zz can be extended inside the vocabulary, it can be extended by one source symbol at a time.

For z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, define the set of one-symbol vocabulary extensions of zz by

Ext𝒵⁡(z):={a∈𝒴:z​a∈𝒵}.\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z):=\left\{a\in\mathcal{Y}:za\in\mathcal{Z}\right\}.

Thus Ext𝒵⁡(z)\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z) is the set of source symbols by which the current token zz can be extended while remaining inside the vocabulary.

For a string s=s1⋯sm∈𝒴∗s=s_{1}\cdots s_{m}\in\mathcal{Y}^{*} with m≥wsm\geq w_{s}, define

sufws⁡(s):=sm−ws+1m.\operatorname{suf}_{w_{s}}(s):=s_{m-w_{s}+1}^{m}.

That is, sufws⁡(s)\operatorname{suf}_{w_{s}}(s) is the suffix of ss of length wsw_{s}.

Given a source-level predictor q∈𝒬ws𝒴q\in\mathcal{Q}_{w_{s}}^{\mathcal{Y}}, define its sequential extension qseqq^{\mathrm{seq}} by

qseq​(u1r∣h):=∏j=1rq⁡(uj|sufws⁡(h​u1j−1)),q^{\mathrm{seq}}(u_{1}^{r}\mid h):=\prod_{j=1}^{r}q\!\left(u_{j}\,\middle|\,\operatorname{suf}_{w_{s}}(hu_{1}^{j-1})\right),

for every u1r∈𝒴∗u_{1}^{r}\in\mathcal{Y}^{*} and every history h∈𝒴∗h\in\mathcal{Y}^{*} with |h|≥ws|h|\geq w_{s}.

We now construct the token-level predictor induced by qq. For readability, write

γ⁡(z):=Γ𝒵​(z),z∈𝒵.\gamma(z):=\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z),\qquad z\in\mathcal{Z}.

For a token context zi−wi−1z_{i-w}^{i-1}, define its expanded source history by

Hi:=Γ𝒵​(zi−wi−1).H_{i}:=\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-w}^{i-1}).

By the definition of ws=ws​(w)w_{s}=w_{s}(w), every valid ww-token context spans at least wsw_{s} source symbols. Hence qseq(⋅∣Hi)q^{\mathrm{seq}}(\cdot\mid H_{i}) is well-defined.

The token predictor must assign probabilities to tokens, not merely to source symbols. Under greedy parsing, a candidate token ziz_{i} is emitted exactly when the source continuation first matches γ⁡(zi)\gamma(z_{i}), and then stops there rather than extending ziz_{i} by another source symbol in Ext𝒵⁡(zi)\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i}). In addition, since the previous token zi−1z_{i-1} has already been emitted, we must condition on the fact that it was not extended; equivalently, the next source symbol is not in Ext𝒵⁡(zi−1)\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-1}).

Define q~∈𝒬w𝒵\tilde{q}\in\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{Z}} by

q~​(zi∣zi−wi−1):={qseq​(γ⁡(zi)∣Hi)​(1−∑a∈Ext𝒵⁡(zi)q⁡(a|sufws⁡(Hi​γ​(zi))))1−∑a∈Ext𝒵⁡(zi−1)q⁡(a|sufws⁡(Hi)),if ​γ​(zi)1∉Ext𝒵⁡(zi−1),0,otherwise.\tilde{q}(z_{i}\mid z_{i-w}^{i-1}):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{q^{\mathrm{seq}}\!\left(\gamma(z_{i})\mid H_{i}\right)\left(1-\sum_{a\in\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i})}q\!\left(a\,\middle|\,\operatorname{suf}_{w_{s}}(H_{i}\gamma(z_{i}))\right)\right)}{1-\sum_{a\in\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-1})}q\!\left(a\,\middle|\,\operatorname{suf}_{w_{s}}(H_{i})\right)},&\text{if }\gamma(z_{i})_{1}\notin\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-1}),\\[12.91663pt] 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Here γ​(zi)1\gamma(z_{i})_{1} denotes the first source symbol of the token ziz_{i}.

The numerator is the probability, under the source predictor qq, that the next emitted token is exactly ziz_{i}: the continuation matches γ⁡(zi)\gamma(z_{i}), and the following source symbol does not extend ziz_{i} to a longer vocabulary token. The denominator conditions on the event that the previous token zi−1z_{i-1} really ended, rather than being extended. The condition

γ​(zi)1∉Ext𝒵⁡(zi−1)\gamma(z_{i})_{1}\notin\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-1})

rules out candidates that could not legally follow zi−1z_{i-1} under greedy parsing.

Because the sets Ext𝒵⁡(z)\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z) contain one-symbol extensions, the extension events in the sums above are disjoint. Moreover, the legal next-token events partition the event that zi−1z_{i-1} is not extended. Therefore the displayed rule defines a valid probability distribution over next tokens.

We also record an important property of the construction. Apart from the identity of the immediately preceding token zi−1z_{i-1}, which is needed to enforce greedy parsing, the predictor q~\tilde{q} depends on the expanded history HiH_{i} only through

sufws⁡(Hi).\operatorname{suf}_{w_{s}}(H_{i}).

Indeed, every occurrence of qq in the definition above is evaluated using only the suffix of length wsw_{s} of the relevant source history. This is the sense in which the transferred predictor uses only the wsw_{s}-symbol source suffix of the token context.

We now verify that the cumulative log-loss matches that of qq up to boundary terms. Fix a source sequence y1ny_{1}^{n}, and let

z1m:=Π𝒵​(y1n)z_{1}^{m}:=\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}}(y_{1}^{n})

be its greedy tokenization. Thus

γ(z1)γ(z2)⋯γ(zm)=y1n.\gamma(z_{1})\gamma(z_{2})\cdots\gamma(z_{m})=y_{1}^{n}.

Note that the normalizing denominators in the construction below are strictly positive on every valid greedy-parsing context. Indeed, if a token z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} is emitted at an interior token boundary, then it cannot be extendable by every source symbol. Otherwise, if Ext𝒵⁡(z)=𝒴\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z)=\mathcal{Y}, the next source symbol would always extend zz to a longer vocabulary element, and greedy parsing would not emit zz at that boundary. Hence, for every emitted interior token zz, there exists at least one a∈𝒴∖Ext𝒵⁡(z)a\in\mathcal{Y}\setminus\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z). Since qq is strictly positive, we have

1−∑a∈Ext𝒵⁡(z)q⁡(a∣c)=∑a∉Ext𝒵⁡(z)q⁡(a∣c)≥λq1-\sum_{a\in\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z)}q(a\mid c)=\sum_{a\notin\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z)}q(a\mid c)\geq\lambda_{q}

for every context c∈𝒴wsc\in\mathcal{Y}^{w_{s}}. Therefore the denominators appearing below are well-defined and bounded away from zero along valid greedy parses. For invalid token contexts, we define the predictor arbitrarily, for instance uniformly over 𝒵\mathcal{Z}.

We ignore the first ww tokens and the corresponding initial source symbols. Since the vocabulary is finite, this initial part has bounded source length depending only on ww and the maximum token length. Its contribution to the cumulative log-loss is therefore an O⁡(1)O(1) boundary term.

For i>wi>w, define

Ri:=1−∑a∈Ext𝒵⁡(zi)q⁡(a|sufws⁡(Γ𝒵​(zi−w+1i))).R_{i}:=1-\sum_{a\in\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i})}q\!\left(a\,\middle|\,\operatorname{suf}_{w_{s}}\!\left(\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-w+1}^{i})\right)\right).

The quantity RiR_{i} is the qq-probability that, after token ziz_{i} has been emitted, greedy parsing stops at ziz_{i} rather than extending it by one more source symbol.

For i>wi>w, we have

Hi​γ​(zi)=Γ𝒵​(zi−wi),Γ𝒵​(zi−w+1i)​ is a suffix of ​Γ𝒵​(zi−wi).H_{i}\gamma(z_{i})=\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-w}^{i}),\qquad\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-w+1}^{i})\text{ is a suffix of }\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-w}^{i}).

Since every ww-token window spans at least wsw_{s} source symbols, the two histories

Γ𝒵​(zi−wi)andΓ𝒵​(zi−w+1i)\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-w}^{i})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-w+1}^{i})

have the same length-wsw_{s} source suffix. Therefore, the no-extension factor in the numerator of q~​(zi∣zi−wi−1)\tilde{q}(z_{i}\mid z_{i-w}^{i-1}) is exactly RiR_{i}, while the normalizing factor in the denominator is exactly Ri−1R_{i-1}. Hence, along the valid greedy parse,

q~​(zi∣zi−wi−1)=qseq​(γ⁡(zi)∣Hi)​RiRi−1.\tilde{q}(z_{i}\mid z_{i-w}^{i-1})=q^{\mathrm{seq}}\!\left(\gamma(z_{i})\mid H_{i}\right)\frac{R_{i}}{R_{i-1}}.

Multiplying over i=w+1,…,mi=w+1,\ldots,m, we obtain

∏i=w+1mq~​(zi∣zi−wi−1)\displaystyle\prod_{i=w+1}^{m}\tilde{q}(z_{i}\mid z_{i-w}^{i-1}) =∏i=w+1mqseq​(γ⁡(zi)∣Hi)​∏i=w+1mRiRi−1\displaystyle=\prod_{i=w+1}^{m}q^{\mathrm{seq}}\!\left(\gamma(z_{i})\mid H_{i}\right)\prod_{i=w+1}^{m}\frac{R_{i}}{R_{i-1}}
=∏i=w+1mqseq​(γ⁡(zi)∣Hi)​RmRw.\displaystyle=\prod_{i=w+1}^{m}q^{\mathrm{seq}}\!\left(\gamma(z_{i})\mid H_{i}\right)\frac{R_{m}}{R_{w}}.

Because qq is strictly positive, each interior stop probability satisfies λq≤Ri≤1\lambda_{q}\leq R_{i}\leq 1. Hence the telescoping factor Rm/RwR_{m}/R_{w} contributes at most a constant

|−log2⁡(Rm/Rw)|≤2​log2⁡(1/λq),\left|-\log_{2}(R_{m}/R_{w})\right|\leq 2\log_{2}(1/\lambda_{q}),

up to the final finite-sequence boundary. Since the vocabulary is finite, the initial and terminal boundary regions contain at most O⁡(1)O(1) source symbols, and their contribution is O⁡(1)O(1).

It remains to identify the first product. Since

γ(z1)γ(z2)⋯γ(zm)=y1n,\gamma(z_{1})\gamma(z_{2})\cdots\gamma(z_{m})=y_{1}^{n},

and since each HiH_{i} contains the same wsw_{s}-symbol source suffix that the source-level predictor qq would use immediately before predicting the symbols of γ⁡(zi)\gamma(z_{i}), we have

∏i=w+1mqseq​(γ⁡(zi)∣Hi)=∏t∈Inq⁡(yt|yt−wst−1),\prod_{i=w+1}^{m}q^{\mathrm{seq}}\!\left(\gamma(z_{i})\mid H_{i}\right)=\prod_{t\in I_{n}}q\!\left(y_{t}\,\middle|\,y_{t-w_{s}}^{t-1}\right),

where InI_{n} is the set of source positions remaining after removing the initial boundary symbols. Hence this product is exactly the source-level probability assigned by qq to y1ny_{1}^{n}, up to boundary terms.

Taking negative logarithms gives

ℓ⁡(q~,Π𝒵​(y1n))=ℓ⁡(q,y1n)+O⁡(1).\ell\!\left(\tilde{q};\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}}(y_{1}^{n})\right)=\ell(q;y_{1}^{n})+O(1).

This proves the predictor-transfer statement. ∎

A.3 Proof of Corollary 4.2

Proof.

Let Pws(⋅∣c)P_{w_{s}}(\cdot\mid c) denote the optimal source-level predictor with context length wsw_{s}, so that

ℒY​(ws)=𝔼⁡[−log2⁡Pws​(Y0∣Y−ws−1)].\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w_{s})=\mathbb{E}\left[-\log_{2}P_{w_{s}}(Y_{0}\mid Y_{-w_{s}}^{-1})\right].

For η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1), define the smoothed predictor

qη​(y∣c):=(1−η)​Pws​(y∣c)+η​1|𝒴|.q_{\eta}(y\mid c):=(1-\eta)P_{w_{s}}(y\mid c)+\eta\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}.

Then qηq_{\eta} is strictly positive, since

qη​(y∣c)≥η|𝒴|.q_{\eta}(y\mid c)\geq\frac{\eta}{|\mathcal{Y}|}.

Therefore Theorem 4.1 applies to qηq_{\eta}. Hence there exists q~η∈𝒬w𝒵\tilde{q}_{\eta}\in\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{Z}} such that the asymptotic tokenized loss of q~η\tilde{q}_{\eta} equals the source-level loss of qηq_{\eta}. Consequently,

ℒZtok​(w)≤LY​(qη).\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(w)\leq L_{Y}(q_{\eta}).

Finally, by dominated convergence on the finite alphabet,

LY​(qη)→ℒY​(ws)as ​η↓0.L_{Y}(q_{\eta})\to\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w_{s})\qquad\text{as }\eta\downarrow 0.

Thus

ℒZtok​(w)≤ℒY​(ws).\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(w)\leq\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w_{s}).

∎

A.4 Proof of Theorem 4.3

Proof.

Let Pws(⋅∣c)P_{w_{s}}(\cdot\mid c) denote the optimal source-level predictor with context length wsw_{s}, so that

ℒY​(ws)=𝔼⁡[−log2⁡Pws​(Y0∣Y−ws−1)].\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w_{s})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\log_{2}P_{w_{s}}(Y_{0}\mid Y_{-w_{s}}^{-1})\right].

For η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1), define the smoothed source predictor

qη​(y∣c):=(1−η)​Pws​(y∣c)+η​1|𝒴|,y∈𝒴,c∈𝒴ws.q_{\eta}(y\mid c):=(1-\eta)P_{w_{s}}(y\mid c)+\eta\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|},\qquad y\in\mathcal{Y},\;c\in\mathcal{Y}^{w_{s}}.

Then qηq_{\eta} is strictly positive, since

qη​(y∣c)≥η|𝒴|∀y∈𝒴,c∈𝒴ws.q_{\eta}(y\mid c)\geq\frac{\eta}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\qquad\forall y\in\mathcal{Y},\;c\in\mathcal{Y}^{w_{s}}.

Therefore, by Theorem 4.1, applied to qηq_{\eta}, there exists a transferred token-level predictor

q~tr,η∈𝒬ws𝒵\tilde{q}_{\mathrm{tr},\eta}\in\mathcal{Q}_{w_{s}}^{\mathcal{Z}}

whose asymptotic per-source-symbol loss equals the source-level loss of qηq_{\eta}:

LZtok​(q~tr,η)=LY​(qη).L_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(\tilde{q}_{\mathrm{tr},\eta})=L_{Y}(q_{\eta}).

Note that here we intentionally chose the window of the transferred token-level predictor to be wsw_{s} so that it surely spans wsw_{s} source symbols to be able to apply Theorem4.1.

We use the suffix-dependence property of the construction in Theorem 4.1: the transferred predictor only needs the last wsw_{s} source symbols contained in the expanded token history. Hence, if a ww-token context zi−wi−1z_{i-w}^{i-1} satisfies

S⁡(zi−wi−1)≥ws,S(z_{i-w}^{i-1})\geq w_{s},

then this ww-token context contains enough source history to evaluate the same prediction rule as q~tr,η\tilde{q}_{\mathrm{tr},\eta}.

Define a ww-context token predictor q~typ,η∈𝒬w𝒵\tilde{q}_{\mathrm{typ},\eta}\in\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{Z}} by

q~typ,η​(zi∣zi−wi−1):={q~tr,η​(zi∣zi−wi−1),if ​S​(zi−wi−1)≥ws,1|𝒵|,if ​S​(zi−wi−1)<ws.\tilde{q}_{\mathrm{typ},\eta}(z_{i}\mid z_{i-w}^{i-1}):=\begin{cases}\tilde{q}_{\mathrm{tr},\eta}(z_{i}\mid z_{i-w}^{i-1}),&\text{if }S(z_{i-w}^{i-1})\geq w_{s},\\[4.30554pt] \dfrac{1}{|\mathcal{Z}|},&\text{if }S(z_{i-w}^{i-1})<w_{s}.\end{cases}

In the first case, the notation q~tr,η​(zi∣zi−wi−1)\tilde{q}_{\mathrm{tr},\eta}(z_{i}\mid z_{i-w}^{i-1}) means that we evaluate the transferred predictor using the length-wsw_{s} source suffix contained in the expanded history Γ𝒵​(zi−wi−1)\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(z_{i-w}^{i-1}).

Let

α𝒵:=𝔼⁡[|Γ𝒵​(Z0)|],\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}:=\mathbb{E}\!\left[|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(Z_{0})|\right],

and define the bad-span event

B:={S(Z−w−1)<ws}.B:=\left\{S(Z_{-w}^{-1})<w_{s}\right\}.

Since the tokenizer is (ϵ,w,ws)(\epsilon,w,w_{s})-typical,

Pr⁡(B)≤ϵ.\Pr(B)\leq\epsilon.

Define the pointwise token losses

ℓtyp,η:=−log2⁡q~typ,η​(Z0∣Z−w−1),\ell_{\mathrm{typ},\eta}:=-\log_{2}\tilde{q}_{\mathrm{typ},\eta}(Z_{0}\mid Z_{-w}^{-1}),

and

ℓtr,η:=−log2⁡q~tr,η​(Z0∣Z−ws−1).\ell_{\mathrm{tr},\eta}:=-\log_{2}\tilde{q}_{\mathrm{tr},\eta}(Z_{0}\mid Z_{-w_{s}}^{-1}).

On the good-span event BcB^{c}, the ww-token context contains the required wsw_{s} source-symbol suffix, so by construction

ℓtyp,η=ℓtr,ηon ​Bc.\ell_{\mathrm{typ},\eta}=\ell_{\mathrm{tr},\eta}\qquad\text{on }B^{c}.

On the bad-span event BB, the predictor q~typ,η\tilde{q}_{\mathrm{typ},\eta} is uniform over 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, and therefore

ℓtyp,η=log2⁡|𝒵|on ​B.\ell_{\mathrm{typ},\eta}=\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|\qquad\text{on }B.

Thus,

LZtok​(q~typ,η)\displaystyle L_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(\tilde{q}_{\mathrm{typ},\eta}) =1α𝒵​𝔼​[ℓtyp,η]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell_{\mathrm{typ},\eta}\right]
=1α𝒵​𝔼​[ℓtyp,η​𝟏Bc]+1α𝒵​𝔼​[ℓtyp,η​𝟏B]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell_{\mathrm{typ},\eta}\mathbf{1}_{B^{c}}\right]+\frac{1}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell_{\mathrm{typ},\eta}\mathbf{1}_{B}\right]
=1α𝒵​𝔼​[ℓtr,η​𝟏Bc]+Pr⁡(B)​log2​|𝒵|α𝒵\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell_{\mathrm{tr},\eta}\mathbf{1}_{B^{c}}\right]+\frac{\Pr(B)\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}}
≤1α𝒵​𝔼​[ℓtr,η]+Pr⁡(B)​log2​|𝒵|α𝒵\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell_{\mathrm{tr},\eta}\right]+\frac{\Pr(B)\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}}
=LZtok​(q~tr,η)+Pr⁡(B)​log2​|𝒵|α𝒵\displaystyle=L_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(\tilde{q}_{\mathrm{tr},\eta})+\frac{\Pr(B)\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}}
≤LY​(qη)+ϵ​log2⁡|𝒵|α𝒵.\displaystyle\leq L_{Y}(q_{\eta})+\epsilon\frac{\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}}.

Since ℒZtok​(w)\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(w) is the minimum loss over 𝒬w𝒵\mathcal{Q}_{w}^{\mathcal{Z}}, we obtain

ℒZtok​(w)≤LY​(qη)+ϵ​log2⁡|𝒵|α𝒵.\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(w)\leq L_{Y}(q_{\eta})+\epsilon\frac{\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}}.

It remains to let η↓0\eta\downarrow 0. For every context cc and symbol yy,

qη​(y∣c)→Pws​(y∣c).q_{\eta}(y\mid c)\to P_{w_{s}}(y\mid c).

Moreover, on the support of Pws(⋅∣c)P_{w_{s}}(\cdot\mid c), for η≤1/2\eta\leq 1/2,

qη​(y∣c)≥(1−η)​Pws​(y∣c)≥12​Pws​(y∣c).q_{\eta}(y\mid c)\geq(1-\eta)P_{w_{s}}(y\mid c)\geq\frac{1}{2}P_{w_{s}}(y\mid c).

Hence

−log2⁡qη​(y∣c)≤−log2⁡Pws​(y∣c)+1-\log_{2}q_{\eta}(y\mid c)\leq-\log_{2}P_{w_{s}}(y\mid c)+1

on the support of PwsP_{w_{s}}. Since the alphabets are finite, dominated convergence gives

LY​(qη)→ℒY​(ws)as ​η↓0.L_{Y}(q_{\eta})\to\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w_{s})\qquad\text{as }\eta\downarrow 0.

Therefore,

ℒZtok​(w)≤ℒY​(ws)+ϵ​log2⁡|𝒵|α𝒵.\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(w)\leq\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w_{s})+\epsilon\frac{\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}}.

Finally, using

R𝒵=log2⁡|𝒵|α𝒵​log2​|𝒴|,R_{\mathcal{Z}}=\frac{\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}\log_{2}|\mathcal{Y}|},

we get

ℒZtok​(w)≤ℒY​(ws)+ϵ​R𝒵​log2​|𝒴|.\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(w)\leq\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w_{s})+\epsilon\,R_{\mathcal{Z}}\log_{2}|\mathcal{Y}|.

This proves the theorem. ∎

Appendix B Existence of Typical Source-Span Tokenizers

In this appendix, we show that the typical source-span condition in Definition 4.1 is satisfied by a class of learned greedy tokenizers under a typical version of the heavy-hitting condition studied by Rajaraman et al. (2024b). The purpose of this appendix is not to reprove their LZW learning result, but to translate high-probability substring coverage into our source-span language.

The conclusion is that, under the same Markov positivity assumption used by Rajaraman et al. (2024b), a learned budget-dd greedy tokenizer satisfying a typical high-probability-continuation coverage condition is

(4​η,w,wd)​-typical,wd:=⌊34​w​ℓd⌋,\left(4\eta,\;w,\;w_{d}\right)\text{-typical},\qquad w_{d}:=\left\lfloor\frac{3}{4}w\ell_{d}\right\rfloor,

where

ℓd:=β​log2​dlog2⁡(1/δ).\ell_{d}:=\frac{\beta\log_{2}d}{\log_{2}(1/\delta)}.

Combining this with Theorem 4.3 gives a finite-context loss guarantee for the learned tokenizer.

B.1 Setup

Let {Yi}i∈ℤ\{Y_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{Z}} be a stationary ergodic kk-th order Markov source over a finite alphabet 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. We write its transition kernel as

P⁡(y∣c),c∈𝒴k,y∈𝒴,P(y\mid c),\qquad c\in\mathcal{Y}^{k},\ y\in\mathcal{Y},

where cc denotes the previous kk source symbols. We assume the following positivity condition.

Assumption 1 (δ\delta-positive kk-th order Markov source).

There exists δ>0\delta>0 such that

minc∈𝒴k,y∈𝒴⁡P⁡(y∣c)≥δ.\min_{c\in\mathcal{Y}^{k},\ y\in\mathcal{Y}}P(y\mid c)\geq\delta.
Remark B.1.

The first-order Markov setting considered by Rajaraman et al. (2024b) extends to the kk-th order setting by treating the length-kk context Yi−ki−1Y_{i-k}^{i-1} as the Markov state. We write the proof directly in kk-th order notation to match the rest of the paper.

For a string u∈𝒴∗u\in\mathcal{Y}^{*} with |u|≥k|u|\geq k, let sufk⁡(u)\operatorname{suf}_{k}(u) denote the length-kk suffix of uu. For a string t=t1⋯tm∈𝒴mt=t_{1}\cdots t_{m}\in\mathcal{Y}^{m} and an initial context c∈𝒴kc\in\mathcal{Y}^{k}, define

P⁡(t∣c):=∏j=1mP⁡(tj|sufk⁡(c​t1j−1)),P(t\mid c):=\prod_{j=1}^{m}P\!\left(t_{j}\,\middle|\,\operatorname{suf}_{k}(c\,t_{1}^{j-1})\right),

where c​t1j−1c\,t_{1}^{j-1} denotes concatenation of the initial context cc and the prefix t1j−1t_{1}^{j-1}. Also define

pmax​(t):=maxc∈𝒴k⁡P⁡(t∣c).p_{\max}(t):=\max_{c\in\mathcal{Y}^{k}}P(t\mid c).

By Assumption 1, every nonempty string tt satisfies

pmax​(t)≥δ|t|.p_{\max}(t)\geq\delta^{|t|}. (6)

Indeed, for every initial context cc, the product defining P⁡(t∣c)P(t\mid c) contains |t||t| transition probabilities, each at least δ\delta. This is the only source-probability estimate we need below.

Let 𝒵⊆𝒴∗\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}^{*} be a finite greedy vocabulary containing all single-symbol strings. As in the main text, Π𝒵\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}} denotes the greedy parser and Γ𝒵\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}} denotes the expansion map. We consider the stationary token process {Zj}\{Z_{j}\} induced by applying Π𝒵\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}} to the stationary source. Recall that

S⁡(Zi−wi−1):=|Γ𝒵​(Zi−wi−1)|=∑j=i−wi−1|Γ𝒵​(Zj)|S(Z_{i-w}^{i-1}):=\left|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(Z_{i-w}^{i-1})\right|=\sum_{j=i-w}^{i-1}|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(Z_{j})|

is the source span of a ww-token context.

B.2 High-probability substrings and typical coverage

For β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), define the high-probability substring set

Mβ:={t∈𝒴∗:pmax​(t)≥δdβ}.M_{\beta}:=\left\{t\in\mathcal{Y}^{*}:p_{\max}(t)\geq\frac{\delta}{d^{\beta}}\right\}.

This is the high-probability region used in the LZW analysis of Rajaraman et al. (2024b). In particular, their Lemma A.10 shows that, under the corresponding Markov positivity assumption, LZW learns all substrings in MβM_{\beta} with high probability for any fixed β<1\beta<1. We use a weaker, typical version of this coverage property.

Let T=Z0T=Z_{0} be a token drawn from the stationary emitted-token distribution. Let A0∈𝒴A_{0}\in\mathcal{Y} denote the next source symbol immediately following the source string Γ𝒵​(T)\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T) in the underlying source sequence. Thus Γ𝒵​(T)​A0\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)A_{0} is the one-symbol continuation of the emitted token along the actual source realization.

Definition B.1 (Typical coverage of high-probability continuations).

A greedy vocabulary 𝒵\mathcal{Z} satisfies (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typical MβM_{\beta}-coverage if

Pr[Γ𝒵(T)A0∈Mβ∖𝒵]≤η.\Pr\!\left[\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)A_{0}\in M_{\beta}\setminus\mathcal{Z}\right]\leq\eta.

This condition says that, at a stationary token boundary, the learned vocabulary usually contains the high-probability one-symbol continuation that would have allowed greedy parsing to extend the current token. It is the typical analogue of the deterministic event Mβ⊆𝒵M_{\beta}\subseteq\mathcal{Z} used in the LZW analysis of Rajaraman et al. (2024b).

Assumption 2 (Typical LZW coverage).

Fix β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) and η≥0\eta\geq 0. Let 𝒵n\mathcal{Z}_{n} be the dictionary learned from tokenizer-training data, with vocabulary budget at most dd. For sufficiently large tokenizer-training data, there exists a failure probability ξn​(d,β,η,δ)\xi_{n}(d,\beta,\eta,\delta), with

ξn​(d,β,η,δ)→0\xi_{n}(d,\beta,\eta,\delta)\to 0

as the tokenizer-training data grows, such that with probability at least 1−ξn​(d,β,η,δ)1-\xi_{n}(d,\beta,\eta,\delta), the learned dictionary 𝒵n\mathcal{Z}_{n} satisfies (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typical MβM_{\beta}-coverage.

Remark B.2.

Assumption 2 is weaker than the deterministic coverage guarantee proved by Rajaraman et al. (2024b). Their Lemma A.10 shows that LZW learns all substrings in MβM_{\beta} with high probability. That deterministic event implies (β,0)(\beta,0)-typical MβM_{\beta}-coverage. Here we state the weaker typical version because our theorem only needs the missed-continuation probability to be small, not zero.

B.3 Typical heavy-hitting

Definition B.2 (Typical heavy-hitting).

A greedy tokenizer 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typically heavy-hitting if

PrT[pmax(Γ𝒵(T))>d−β]≤η.\Pr_{T}\!\left[p_{\max}\!\left(\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)\right)>d^{-\beta}\right]\leq\eta.
Lemma B.1 (Typical coverage implies typical heavy-hitting).

If 𝒵\mathcal{Z} satisfies (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typical MβM_{\beta}-coverage, then 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typically heavy-hitting.

Proof.

Let T=Z0T=Z_{0} be a stationary emitted token, and let A0A_{0} be the next source symbol after Γ𝒵​(T)\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T) in the underlying source sequence.

Suppose that

pmax​(Γ𝒵​(T))>d−β.p_{\max}\!\left(\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)\right)>d^{-\beta}.

Then there exists a length-kk context c⋆∈𝒴kc^{\star}\in\mathcal{Y}^{k} such that

P⁡(Γ𝒵​(T)∣c⋆)>d−β.P(\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)\mid c^{\star})>d^{-\beta}.

Let

cT:=sufk⁡(c⋆​Γ𝒵​(T))c_{T}:=\operatorname{suf}_{k}\!\left(c^{\star}\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)\right)

be the length-kk context that would precede the next source symbol after generating Γ𝒵​(T)\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T) from the initial context c⋆c^{\star}. By Assumption 1,

P⁡(A0∣cT)≥δ.P(A_{0}\mid c_{T})\geq\delta.

Therefore,

P⁡(Γ𝒵​(T)​A0∣c⋆)=P⁡(Γ𝒵​(T)∣c⋆)​P​(A0∣cT)>δdβ.P(\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)A_{0}\mid c^{\star})=P(\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)\mid c^{\star})P(A_{0}\mid c_{T})>\frac{\delta}{d^{\beta}}.

Hence

pmax​(Γ𝒵​(T)​A0)>δdβ,p_{\max}\!\left(\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)A_{0}\right)>\frac{\delta}{d^{\beta}},

and therefore

Γ𝒵​(T)​A0∈Mβ.\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)A_{0}\in M_{\beta}.

On the other hand, greedy parsing emitted TT rather than a longer token. Since Γ𝒵​(T)​A0\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)A_{0} is a longer string matching the current source position, it cannot belong to 𝒵\mathcal{Z}; otherwise greedy parsing would have continued beyond TT. Thus

Γ𝒵​(T)​A0∈Mβ∖𝒵.\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)A_{0}\in M_{\beta}\setminus\mathcal{Z}.

We have shown the event inclusion

{pmax(Γ𝒵(T))>d−β}⊆{Γ𝒵(T)A0∈Mβ∖𝒵}.\left\{p_{\max}\!\left(\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)\right)>d^{-\beta}\right\}\subseteq\left\{\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)A_{0}\in M_{\beta}\setminus\mathcal{Z}\right\}.

Taking probabilities and using Definition B.1 gives

PrT[pmax(Γ𝒵(T))>d−β]≤η.\Pr_{T}\!\left[p_{\max}\!\left(\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)\right)>d^{-\beta}\right]\leq\eta.

Thus 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typically heavy-hitting. ∎

Corollary B.2 (Existence of typically heavy-hitting learned tokenizers).

Under Assumptions 1 and 2, with probability at least 1−ξn​(d,β,η,δ)1-\xi_{n}(d,\beta,\eta,\delta) over the tokenizer-training data, the learned greedy tokenizer 𝒵n\mathcal{Z}_{n} is (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typically heavy-hitting.

Proof.

By Assumption 2, with probability at least 1−ξn​(d,β,η,δ)1-\xi_{n}(d,\beta,\eta,\delta), the learned dictionary satisfies (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typical MβM_{\beta}-coverage. Lemma B.1 then implies that 𝒵n\mathcal{Z}_{n} is (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typically heavy-hitting. ∎

B.4 From typical heavy-hitting to typical source span

We now prove the part specific to our paper: typical heavy-hitting implies the typical source-span condition in Definition 4.1.

Lemma B.3 (Typical heavy-hitting implies long tokens with high probability).

Assume 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typically heavy-hitting. Define

ℓd:=β​log2​dlog2⁡(1/δ).\ell_{d}:=\frac{\beta\log_{2}d}{\log_{2}(1/\delta)}.

Then

PrT[|Γ𝒵(T)|<ℓd]≤η.\Pr_{T}\!\left[|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)|<\ell_{d}\right]\leq\eta.
Proof.

Call a token TT good if

pmax​(Γ𝒵​(T))≤d−β.p_{\max}\!\left(\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)\right)\leq d^{-\beta}.

By Definition B.2,

PrT⁡[T​ is not good]≤η.\Pr_{T}[T\text{ is not good}]\leq\eta.

If TT is good, then by (6),

δ|Γ𝒵​(T)|≤pmax​(Γ𝒵​(T))≤d−β.\delta^{|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)|}\leq p_{\max}\!\left(\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)\right)\leq d^{-\beta}.

Taking logarithms gives

|Γ𝒵​(T)|≥β​log2​dlog2⁡(1/δ)=ℓd.|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)|\geq\frac{\beta\log_{2}d}{\log_{2}(1/\delta)}=\ell_{d}.

Therefore the event

|Γ𝒵​(T)|<ℓd|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)|<\ell_{d}

can occur only when TT is not good. Hence

PrT[|Γ𝒵(T)|<ℓd]≤η.\Pr_{T}\!\left[|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(T)|<\ell_{d}\right]\leq\eta.

∎

Lemma B.4 (Typical heavy-hitting implies typical source span).

Assume 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typically heavy-hitting. Fix a token-window length ww, and define

ℓd:=β​log2​dlog2⁡(1/δ).\ell_{d}:=\frac{\beta\log_{2}d}{\log_{2}(1/\delta)}.

Let

wd:=⌊34​w​ℓd⌋.w_{d}:=\left\lfloor\frac{3}{4}w\ell_{d}\right\rfloor.

Then

Pr[S(Zi−wi−1)<wd]≤4η.\Pr\!\left[S(Z_{i-w}^{i-1})<w_{d}\right]\leq 4\eta.

Equivalently, Π𝒵\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}} is

(4​η,w,wd)​-typical.\left(4\eta,\;w,\;w_{d}\right)\text{-typical}.
Proof.

For each token ZjZ_{j}, define the bad-token indicator

Bj:=𝟏{|Γ𝒵(Zj)|<ℓd}.B_{j}:=\mathbf{1}\left\{|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(Z_{j})|<\ell_{d}\right\}.

By Lemma B.3,

𝔼⁡[Bj]=Pr⁡(Bj=1)≤η.\mathbb{E}[B_{j}]=\Pr(B_{j}=1)\leq\eta.

For the window Zi−wi−1Z_{i-w}^{i-1}, let

B:=∑j=i−wi−1BjB:=\sum_{j=i-w}^{i-1}B_{j}

be the number of bad tokens in the window. By linearity of expectation,

𝔼⁡[B]≤w​η.\mathbb{E}[B]\leq w\eta.

Every good token has source length at least ℓd\ell_{d}, and every bad token has source length at least 11. Therefore,

S⁡(Zi−wi−1)=∑j=i−wi−1|Γ𝒵​(Zj)|≥(w−B)​ℓd+B.S(Z_{i-w}^{i-1})=\sum_{j=i-w}^{i-1}|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(Z_{j})|\geq(w-B)\ell_{d}+B.

In particular, if B≤w/4B\leq w/4, then

S⁡(Zi−wi−1)≥(w−w4)​ℓd=34​w​ℓd≥wd.S(Z_{i-w}^{i-1})\geq\left(w-\frac{w}{4}\right)\ell_{d}=\frac{3}{4}w\ell_{d}\geq w_{d}.

Thus,

{S(Zi−wi−1)<wd}⊆{B>w4}.\left\{S(Z_{i-w}^{i-1})<w_{d}\right\}\subseteq\left\{B>\frac{w}{4}\right\}.

By Markov’s inequality,

Pr[B>w4]≤𝔼⁡[B]w/4≤4η.\Pr\!\left[B>\frac{w}{4}\right]\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[B]}{w/4}\leq 4\eta.

Therefore,

Pr[S(Zi−wi−1)<wd]≤4η.\Pr\!\left[S(Z_{i-w}^{i-1})<w_{d}\right]\leq 4\eta.

This is exactly the (4​η,w,wd)\left(4\eta,w,w_{d}\right)-typicality condition. ∎

B.5 Tokenizer rate bound

We also need to control the rate term in Theorem 4.3. Recall that

α𝒵:=𝔼⁡[|Γ𝒵​(Z0)|]\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}:=\mathbb{E}\!\left[|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(Z_{0})|\right]

and

R𝒵:=log2⁡|𝒵|α𝒵​log2​|𝒴|.R_{\mathcal{Z}}:=\frac{\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}\log_{2}|\mathcal{Y}|}.
Lemma B.5 (Rate bound for typically heavy-hitting tokenizers).

Assume 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typically heavy-hitting and |𝒵|≤d|\mathcal{Z}|\leq d. Then

α𝒵≥(1−η)​ℓd+η,\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}\geq(1-\eta)\ell_{d}+\eta,

where

ℓd:=β​log2​dlog2⁡(1/δ).\ell_{d}:=\frac{\beta\log_{2}d}{\log_{2}(1/\delta)}.

Consequently,

R𝒵≤log2⁡d((1−η)​ℓd+η)​log2​|𝒴|.R_{\mathcal{Z}}\leq\frac{\log_{2}d}{\big((1-\eta)\ell_{d}+\eta\big)\log_{2}|\mathcal{Y}|}.
Proof.

By Lemma B.3, with probability at least 1−η1-\eta, an emitted token has source length at least ℓd\ell_{d}. On the remaining event, the token has source length at least 11, since all tokens are nonempty source strings. Hence

α𝒵=𝔼⁡[|Γ𝒵​(Z0)|]≥(1−η)​ℓd+η.\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[|\Gamma_{\mathcal{Z}}(Z_{0})|\right]\geq(1-\eta)\ell_{d}+\eta.

Since |𝒵|≤d|\mathcal{Z}|\leq d,

R𝒵=log2⁡|𝒵|α𝒵​log2​|𝒴|≤log2⁡d((1−η)​ℓd+η)​log2​|𝒴|.R_{\mathcal{Z}}=\frac{\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}\log_{2}|\mathcal{Y}|}\leq\frac{\log_{2}d}{\big((1-\eta)\ell_{d}+\eta\big)\log_{2}|\mathcal{Y}|}.

∎

B.6 Main result

We now combine the existence of a typically heavy-hitting dictionary with the source-span and rate bounds above.

Theorem B.6 (Existence of tokenizers with typical effective context).

Assume {Yi}\{Y_{i}\} satisfies Assumption 1. Fix β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), vocabulary budget dd, token-window length ww, and η∈[0,1/4]\eta\in[0,1/4]. Define

ℓd:=β​log2​dlog2⁡(1/δ)\ell_{d}:=\frac{\beta\log_{2}d}{\log_{2}(1/\delta)}

and

wd:=⌊34​w​ℓd⌋.w_{d}:=\left\lfloor\frac{3}{4}w\ell_{d}\right\rfloor.

For sufficiently large tokenizer-training data, with probability at least 1−ξn​(d,β,η,δ)1-\xi_{n}(d,\beta,\eta,\delta) over the training sequence, the learned LZW tokenizer Π𝒵n\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}_{n}} is

(4​η,w,wd)​-typical.\left(4\eta,\;w,\;w_{d}\right)\text{-typical}.

Moreover,

R𝒵n≤log2⁡d((1−η)​ℓd+η)​log2​|𝒴|.R_{\mathcal{Z}_{n}}\leq\frac{\log_{2}d}{\big((1-\eta)\ell_{d}+\eta\big)\log_{2}|\mathcal{Y}|}.

Consequently,

ℒZtok​(w)≤ℒY​(wd)+4​η​R𝒵n​log2​|𝒴|.\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(w)\leq\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w_{d})+4\eta\,R_{\mathcal{Z}_{n}}\log_{2}|\mathcal{Y}|.

In particular,

ℒZtok​(w)≤ℒY​(wd)+4​η​log2⁡d(1−η)​ℓd+η.\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(w)\leq\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w_{d})+4\eta\frac{\log_{2}d}{(1-\eta)\ell_{d}+\eta}.
Proof.

By Corollary B.2, with probability at least 1−ξn​(d,β,η,δ)1-\xi_{n}(d,\beta,\eta,\delta), the learned LZW dictionary 𝒵n\mathcal{Z}_{n} is (β,η)(\beta,\eta)-typically heavy-hitting. On this event, Lemma B.4 gives

Pr[S(Zi−wi−1)<wd]≤4η.\Pr\!\left[S(Z_{i-w}^{i-1})<w_{d}\right]\leq 4\eta.

Therefore Π𝒵n\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}_{n}} is

(4​η,w,wd)​-typical.\left(4\eta,\;w,\;w_{d}\right)\text{-typical}.

Also, by Lemma B.5,

R𝒵n≤log2⁡d((1−η)​ℓd+η)​log2​|𝒴|.R_{\mathcal{Z}_{n}}\leq\frac{\log_{2}d}{\big((1-\eta)\ell_{d}+\eta\big)\log_{2}|\mathcal{Y}|}.

Now apply Theorem 4.3 with

ϵ=4​ηandws=wd.\epsilon=4\eta\qquad\text{and}\qquad w_{s}=w_{d}.

This gives

ℒZtok​(w)≤ℒY​(wd)+4​η​R𝒵n​log2​|𝒴|.\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(w)\leq\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w_{d})+4\eta\,R_{\mathcal{Z}_{n}}\log_{2}|\mathcal{Y}|.

Substituting the rate bound yields

ℒZtok​(w)≤ℒY​(wd)+4​η​log2⁡d(1−η)​ℓd+η.\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\mathrm{tok}}(w)\leq\mathcal{L}_{Y}(w_{d})+4\eta\frac{\log_{2}d}{(1-\eta)\ell_{d}+\eta}.

∎

Remark B.3.

The LZW guarantee of Rajaraman et al. (2024b) gives a stronger deterministic sufficient condition: with high probability, LZW learns all substrings in MβM_{\beta}, which implies (β,0)(\beta,0)-typical MβM_{\beta}-coverage. We state the result using the weaker typical-coverage condition because Theorem 4.3 is naturally a typical-span theorem: it only requires the window-span failure probability to be small, not zero.

Appendix C Implementation Details

All experiments are implemented in PyTorch and run on a single NVIDIA GPU (CUDA 12.8). The full code, configs, and scripts needed to reproduce every figure in the paper are available at the following anonymous repository:

https://github.com/Amiroo23jf/bytes-are-not-enough

C.1 Transformer Architecture

Both the fragmentation and tokenization experiments use the same causal transformer architecture, differing only in embedding dimension and feedforward width. The model is a standard pre-norm transformer with sinusoidal positional encodings, GELU activations, and no weight tying between the input embedding and the output projection. All linear layers are bias-free; attention is implemented with scaled_dot_product_attention. Weights are initialised from 𝒩⁡(0, 0.022)\mathcal{N}(0,\,0.02^{2}).

C.2 Fragmentation Transformer Experiment

Source.

We generate a binary Markov source of order K=2K=2 with fragment alphabet size 2M=82^{M}=8 (M=3M=3). The transition matrix PP is drawn from a symmetric Dirichlet prior with concentration α=0.5\alpha=0.5. The source sequence length is n=2×106n=2\times 10^{6} symbols per run.

Context window.

We set W=K+1=3W=K+1=3. With this choice the oracle-residual term in Theorem 1 vanishes, so the gap between the fragment-level and source-level Bayes-optimal losses equals exactly the phase mutual-information term.

Training.

We train both the YY-model (fragment-level) and the XX-model (source-level) independently. Each model is trained for 40 000 gradient steps with the AdamW optimiser (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) using the hyperparameters in Table 2. Loss curves are smoothed with a trailing window of 500 steps for plotting. All results are averaged over 3 independent seeds; shaded bands show ±1\pm 1 standard deviation.

C.3 Tokenization Transformer Experiment

Source.

We generate a binary Markov source of order K=12K=12 with Dirichlet concentration α=0.4\alpha=0.4 and source length n=2.5×107n=2.5\times 10^{7} bits. One sequence is generated per seed and shared across all (V,W)(V,W) combinations within that seed.

BPE tokenizer.

For each vocabulary size V>2V>2 we train a greedy BPE tokenizer on the first 5×1055\times 10^{5} bits of the source sequence. For V=2V=2 the source is used directly without tokenisation (ratio =1=1). The compression ratios achieved for the full source sequence are reported in Table 3.

Sweep.

We sweep vocabulary sizes V∈{2,4,6,8,10,15,20}V\in\{2,4,6,8,10,15,20\} and context window W∈{4,6,12}W\in\{4,6,12\}, training one model per (V,W,seed)(V,W,\text{seed}) triple. All models share the architecture in Table 1. Loss is reported in bits per source symbol: the raw cross-entropy is divided by the token-level compression ratio so that all vocabulary sizes are on a common scale.

Training.

Training hyperparameters are given in Table 4. Results are averaged over 3 seeds; shaded bands show ±1\pm 1 standard deviation.

C.4 Fragmentation N-gram Experiment

We verify Theorem 3.1 empirically with a kk-th order nn-gram model on a binary Markov source. For each pair (k,M)(k,M) in {(1,2),(1,3),(1,4),(2,2),(2,3),(3,2)}\{(1,2),(1,3),(1,4),(2,2),(2,3),(3,2)\} we sample 8 transition matrices independently from a symmetric Dirichlet prior (α=0.5\alpha=0.5) and generate a source sequence of n=5×105n=5\times 10^{5} symbols per matrix. We fit two nn-gram models: one with context length K=kK=k (exact match) and one with K=k+1K=k+1 (one extra token of context). Counts are smoothed with Laplace smoothing (α=0.5\alpha=0.5). The theoretical excess loss from Theorem 3.1 is computed analytically from the sampled transition matrix and compared to the empirical nn-gram loss.

C.5 Span-Distribution Analysis

WikiText-103.

We measure P⁡(span⁡(ZW)=ws)P(\mathrm{span}(Z^{W})=w_{s})—the distribution of source characters covered by WW consecutive tokens—for the following tokenizers trained on WikiText-103 (Merity et al., 2017): character, BPE with |V|∈{1​k,4​k,16​k,32​k}|V|\in\{1\mathrm{k},4\mathrm{k},16\mathrm{k},32\mathrm{k}\}, WordPiece (32k), SentencePiece (32k), BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), and GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019). We sweep W∈{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256}W\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256\}.

Markov source.

We repeat the same analysis on the synthetic binary Markov source used in the tokenization transformer experiment (K=12K=12, α=0.4\alpha=0.4, n=2.5×107n=2.5\times 10^{7}, seed 0), using the BPE tokenizers trained for that experiment (V∈{2,4,6,8,10,15,20}V\in\{2,4,6,8,10,15,20\}). Here the span wsw_{s} is measured in source bits rather than characters, and we sweep W∈{1,…,12}W\in\{1,\ldots,12\}. The plotted quantity is the scaled CDF ε⁡(ws)⋅log2⁡V⋅𝔼⁡[|Z|/|Y|]\varepsilon(w_{s})\cdot\log_{2}V\cdot\mathbb{E}[|Z|/|Y|], which provides a normalised upper bound comparable across tokenizers.

Appendix D Additional Experiments

D.1 Fragmentation Decomposition

We empirically verify the decomposition in Theorem 3.1 using finite-order Markov sources under several parameter settings. For each configuration, we compare the optimal source-level loss with the normalized loss after fragmentation, and then compare the observed fragmentation penalty with the theoretical decomposition into phase ambiguity and context deficit.

Figure 6 shows the results across four source regimes. In each row, the left panel reports the per-source-symbol loss: the theoretical source entropy, the empirical nn-gram loss on the original source sequence, and the normalized nn-gram loss on the fragmented sequence. The right panel reports the penalty decomposition. The empirical penalty matches the predicted total penalty, showing that the excess loss observed after fragmentation is explained by the information-theoretic terms in Theorem 3.1.

D.2 Matched-Plateau Comparisons

Figure 7 compares vocabulary/window pairs that reach approximately the same plateau loss. The tokenized configurations achieve this plateau with much smaller token windows than the binary baseline, and they also reach it in fewer training iterations. This suggests that, in this synthetic setting, tokenization improves both effective context and convergence speed.

D.3 Tokenizer Source-Span Distributions Across Window Sizes

We also evaluate the source-span behavior of real tokenizers on WikiText across several token-window lengths. For each tokenizer and window size ww, we estimate the distribution of the source span S⁡(Z1w)S(Z_{1}^{w}) and the corresponding slack term from Theorem 4.3,

ϵ(w,ws)log2⁡|𝒵|α𝒵,ϵ(w,ws)=Pr[S(Z1w)<ws].\epsilon(w,w_{s})\frac{\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|}{\alpha_{\mathcal{Z}}},\qquad\epsilon(w,w_{s})=\Pr[S(Z_{1}^{w})<w_{s}].

Figures 8 and 9 show that the same qualitative behavior persists across window sizes: tokenized windows reliably span substantially more source characters than the raw character window, and the slack remains small until the requested source span grows well beyond ww.
